  %\VignetteIndexEntry{KARST on a Simulated GRF Landscape}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}

---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(karst)
```

Generate a lightweight paper-style GRF truth landscape. The object stores GRF
centroids and computes fitness only for requested karyotypes.

```{r landscape}
landscape <- simulate_grf_landscape(
  n_chr = 4,
  n_centroids = 12,
  lambda = 0.8,
  min_cn = 1,
  max_cn = 4,
  seed = 10
)
predict_landscape_fitness(landscape, matrix(c(2, 2, 2, 2), nrow = 1))
```

Simulate sparse two-timepoint data from the known landscape.

```{r simulate}
sim <- simulate_sparse_counts(
  landscape,
  beta = 0.00005,
  n0 = 150,
  n1 = 150,
  detection_threshold = 1,
  seed = 20,
  initial_population = 500
)
sim$sparsity
```

Fit the sparse joint count model. `fit_karst()` passes the arguments in
`sparse_joint_control` on to `fit_sparse_joint()`.

```{r fit}
fit <- fit_karst(
  sim$counts,
  dt = 1,
  beta = 0.00005,
  sparse_joint_control = list(min_cn = 1, max_cn = 4)
)
fit
head(fit$summary[, c("karyotype", "major", "shell", "relative_fitness", "relative_sd")])
```

Compare with the truth. The simulator's truth is the birth rate, and the
model reports net growth rates, which are smaller by the factor
`2 P_ii - 1` (about 0.9992 for 2.2.2.2 at this missegregation rate); relative to the majors'
count-weighted mean the two agree up to that factor.

```{r truth}
s <- fit$summary
cells <- s$count_t0 + s$count_t1
truth <- predict_landscape_fitness(landscape, s$karyotype)
truth <- truth - weighted.mean(truth[s$major], cells[s$major])
group <- ifelse(s$major, "major", ifelse(cells > 0, "observed, not major", "unobserved"))
aggregate(cbind(fitted = s$relative_fitness, truth = truth, relative_sd = s$relative_sd) ~ group,
          data = data.frame(group, s, truth), FUN = median)
shell <- length(fit$trend$coefficients)
c(shell_coefficient = fit$trend$coefficients[[shell]],
  sd = sqrt(fit$trend$covariance[shell, shell]))
```

With 150 cells per time point and one unit of time between them, the counts
say little about the unobserved neighbours. Their fitness comes mostly from
the shell term of the trend, the distance to the nearest major, whose
coefficient is uncertain: a single cell of a neighbour at the second time
point can move it, and with it every unobserved neighbour, even above the
clones. Their `relative_sd` is correspondingly wide. More cells per time
point or a longer interval constrain them better.

Predict the fitness of any karyotype: inside the fitted domain from the
posterior, outside it from the fitted trend.

```{r predict}
predict(fit, c("2.2.2.2", "3.3.3.3"))[, c("karyotype", "relative_fitness", "relative_sd", "in_domain")]
```
